chunks: From the man (al-Ukhu), from his father, from Ali, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurara, who said:

I said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him): 'My garment was affected by blood from a nosebleed or otherwise, or by some semen. Prayer time arrived and I forgot that there was something on my garment, so I prayed, and then I remembered afterwards?' He said: 'You repeat the prayer and wash it.' I said: 'If I only suspect that it affected it and am not certain of that, and I looked but found nothing, then I searched for it and found it on my garment after the prayer?' He said: 'You wash it and do not repeat the prayer.' I said: 'Why is that?' He said: 'Because you were certain of its purity, then you doubted; so it is not appropriate for you to overturn certainty with doubt ever.' I said: 'What if I see it on my garment while I am praying?' He said: 'You break the prayer and repeat it if you had doubt about its location, then you see it in it. And if you had no doubt, then you see it wet, you cut it off and wash it, then you continue with the prayer, because you do not know perhaps it is something that fell on you; so it is not appropriate for you to overturn certainty with doubt.'
ai.seo_question: What are the rules for repeating prayer if impurity is found on clothing after praying?
ai.summary: This hadith from the *Al-Ullal* tradition illustrates the foundational Shia jurisprudential principle of *al-istishab* (presumption of continuity), where Zarara clarifies that a state of ritual purity is maintained until proven otherwise. It distinguishes between *yaqin* (certainty) and *shakk* (doubt), ruling that doubt does not invalidate certainty unless the impurity is confirmed during the prayer, thereby emphasizing the stability of the believer's worship status.
